wheat.water_needs: Moderate — 4 to 6 irrigations across the season; critical watering at tillering, flowering, and grain-filling stages
common_issues: Yellow Rust (Kundal) — appears as yellow streaks on leaves in cool, humid weather
Brown Rust (Bharti) — small brown pustules on leaves, worsens in warm humid conditions
Loose Smut (Kanak) — black powder replaces grain heads
Aphids (Cheentee) — tiny sap-sucking insects that weaken plants near heading
Army Worm (Lashkari Idda) — caterpillars that chew through leaves and stems
wheat.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~50 kg/acre DAP at sowing + ~50 kg/acre Urea split into 2 doses (at first irrigation and at booting). Adjust based on soil test results.
general_tips: Use certified seed varieties suited to your zone (e.g. Faisalabad-08, Pakistan-13 for Punjab; TD-1 for Sindh).
Sow at the recommended time for your region — late sowing drastically reduces yield due to heat stress at grain filling.
Ensure good land preparation with 2–3 ploughings and planking for even germination.

rice.sowing_season: Nursery: May – June; Transplanting: June – July (Kharif season)
rice.water_needs: High — standing water (5–7 cm) is maintained for most of the growing period; requires reliable irrigation or monsoon rains
common_issues: Blast Disease (Darakht ki Bimari) — diamond-shaped lesions on leaves and neck rot on panicles
Bacterial Leaf Blight — yellowing and wilting of leaf margins
Stem Borer (Tana Chedak) — larvae tunnel into stems causing dead hearts and white heads
Brown Plant Hopper (BPH) — small insects at the base causing hopper burn (drying of plants)
Sheath Blight — oval greenish-grey lesions on leaf sheaths near water level
rice.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~60 kg/acre Urea in 3 split doses (at transplanting, tillering, and panicle initiation). Add ~25 kg/acre DAP at transplanting. Zinc sulphate (6 kg/acre) helps in deficient soils.
general_tips: Transplant 20–25 day old seedlings at a spacing of 20 × 20 cm for better tillering.
Drain the field 10–15 days before harvest to allow uniform ripening and easier harvesting.
Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) can save up to 30% water without significant yield loss.

cotton.sowing_season: April – June (Kharif season); May is ideal for most of Punjab and Sindh
cotton.water_needs: Moderate to High — requires 6–8 irrigations; most critical during flowering and boll formation; avoid waterlogging
common_issues: Cotton Leaf Curl Virus (CLCV / Peeliya) — leaves curl upward, veins thicken; spread by whitefly
Bollworms (Ameri Sundi / Pink Bollworm) — larvae bore into bolls, damaging fibre and seed
Whitefly (Safed Makkhi) — tiny white insects that suck sap and transmit CLCV
Jassids (Tatti) — wedge-shaped insects causing leaf hopper burn (reddening of leaf margins)
Root Rot / Stem Rot — wilting and death of plants in waterlogged soils
cotton.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~50 kg/acre DAP + ~25 kg/acre SOP (sulphate of potash) at sowing. Top dress with ~50 kg/acre Urea in 2 splits at flowering and boll formation. Potash helps boll size and fibre quality.
general_tips: Plant CLCV-resistant varieties (e.g. FH-142, IUB-13, Neelum) to reduce virus damage.
Use pheromone traps to monitor bollworm populations and time sprays more effectively.
Pick cotton at the right maturity — over-due picking leads to fibre contamination and lower grades.

sugarcane.sowing_season: February – March (spring planting) or September – October (autumn planting)
sugarcane.harvesting_season: November – March (10–12 months after spring planting; 15–18 months for autumn)
sugarcane.water_needs: High — sugarcane is a long-duration crop needing 15–20 irrigations; most critical during grand growth phase (June – September)
common_issues: Red Rot (Laal Sarr) — internal reddening of stems, sour smell; a serious fungal disease
Smut (Kaalaa Sir) — black whip-like growths replace the growing point
Top Borer — larvae bore into the top growing shoot causing dead hearts
Early Shoot Borer — attacks young shoots in the first 2 months, causing wilting
Woolly Aphid (Ooni Sussak) — white woolly masses on leaves, weakens the plant
sugarcane.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~100 kg/acre Urea + ~50 kg/acre DAP + ~50 kg/acre SOP at planting. Side dress with ~50 kg/acre Urea at earthing up (90–100 days). Sugarcane is a heavy feeder — soil testing is highly recommended.
general_tips: Use healthy, disease-free seed cane (setts with 2–3 buds) from a reputable source.
Earthing up at 90–120 days prevents lodging (falling over) during monsoon winds.
Trash mulching (spreading dry leaves between rows) conserves moisture and suppresses weeds.

maize.sowing_season: Spring: February – March; Kharif: July – August
maize.harvesting_season: Spring crop: May – June; Kharif crop: September – November
maize.water_needs: Moderate — 4–6 irrigations; most critical at tasselling and silking stages; maize is sensitive to both drought and waterlogging
common_issues: Fall Armyworm (FAW / Lashkari Idda) — larvae eat leaves and bore into cobs; a major recent pest in Pakistan
Downy Mildew — white downy growth on leaves; seedling disease in humid conditions
Corn Borer (Tana Chedak) — larvae tunnel into stems and cobs
Northern Leaf Blight — long grey-green lesions on leaves, reduces grain fill
Storage Weevils (Sussi) — post-harvest grain damage in storage
maize.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~50 kg/acre DAP + ~25 kg/acre SOP at sowing. Side dress ~50 kg/acre Urea in 2 splits: at knee-high stage (25–30 days) and at tasselling. Zinc sulphate (5 kg/acre) improves yield on deficient soils.
general_tips: Plant at 20–25 cm spacing within rows and 60–75 cm between rows for optimal plant population (~30,000 plants/acre).
For FAW control, monitor early and spray with chlorantraniliprole or emamectin benzoate when larvae are young (small).
Harvest when grain moisture is around 20–25% (black layer visible at the base of kernels) and dry to 14% before storage.

potato.sowing_season: October – November (main crop in Punjab); January in Sindh
potato.harvesting_season: January – March (main crop); about 90–120 days after sowing
potato.water_needs: Moderate — frequent light irrigations (every 7–10 days); avoid waterlogging which causes tuber rot; reduce watering near harvest
common_issues: Late Blight (Phitophthora / Jhulsa) — dark water-soaked lesions on leaves spreading rapidly; the most destructive potato disease
Early Blight (Alternaria) — concentric ring spots on older leaves
Black Scurf (Rhizoctonia) — black hard sclerotia on tubers, stem canker
Aphids and Whiteflies — transmit viral diseases causing leaf roll and mosaic
Tuber Moth (Phthorimaea) — larvae tunnel into tubers in the field and in storage
potato.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~60 kg/acre DAP + ~50 kg/acre SOP + ~50 kg/acre Urea at planting as a basal dose. Top dress with ~25 kg/acre Urea at earthing up (30–40 days). Potassium is important for tuber size and quality.
general_tips: Use disease-free certified seed potatoes; cut large tubers into pieces with at least 1–2 eyes and let them cure for a day before planting.
Earth up at 30–40 days to cover developing tubers — this prevents greening (sunlight exposure turns potatoes green and bitter).
Apply preventive fungicide sprays (e.g. mancozeb) before blight appears, especially during cool humid weather.

tomato.sowing_season: Nursery: June – July (for autumn crop) or October – November (for spring crop); transplanting 3–4 weeks later
tomato.harvesting_season: Autumn crop: August – October; Spring crop: December – March
tomato.water_needs: Moderate — regular irrigation every 5–7 days; avoid overhead watering to reduce disease; drip irrigation gives best results
common_issues: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) — leaves curl and yellow, stunted growth; spread by whitefly
Late Blight — dark lesions on leaves, stems, and fruits during cool wet weather
Fruit Borer (Helicoverpa) — larvae bore into fruits making them unmarketable
Fusarium Wilt / Verticillium Wilt — yellowing and wilting from the base upward; soil-borne
Powdery Mildew — white powdery coating on leaves in dry warm conditions
tomato.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~40 kg/acre DAP + ~30 kg/acre SOP + ~25 kg/acre Urea at transplanting. Side dress ~25 kg/acre Urea in 2 splits at flowering and fruiting. Calcium sprays help prevent blossom end rot.
general_tips: Stake or trellis plants to keep fruit off the ground — this reduces disease and improves fruit quality.
Mulch with black plastic or straw to conserve moisture, suppress weeds, and keep soil temperature even.
Pick fruits at the pink (breaker) stage for distant markets — they will ripen fully off the vine with less damage.

onion.sowing_season: Nursery: September – October; transplanting: October – November (Rabi season)
onion.water_needs: Moderate — light frequent irrigations; stop irrigation 10–15 days before harvest to allow bulbs to mature and develop dry outer scales
common_issues: Purple Blotch (Alternaria) — purple-brown spots on leaves that enlarge and kill leaf tips
Stemphylium Blight — yellowish spots turning brown to black on leaves; worsens in humid weather
Downy Mildew — pale green to yellow patches with grey-purple fuzzy growth on leaves
Onion Thrips (Thrips) — tiny slender insects causing silvering of leaf surfaces
Onion Maggot — small white larvae that feed on roots and bulbs, causing rot
onion.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance: apply ~50 kg/acre DAP + ~40 kg/acre SOP + ~25 kg/acre Urea at transplanting. Top dress ~25 kg/acre Urea at 45–60 days. Avoid excess nitrogen late in the season — it delays maturity and causes thick necks (poor storage quality).
general_tips: Transplant seedlings when they are pencil-thick (about 6–8 weeks old) for best bulb size.
Stop irrigation 10–15 days before harvest and allow tops to fall over naturally — this improves bulb curing and storage life.
Cure harvested onions in the shade for 7–10 days (until necks are tight and outer scales are dry) before storage.

mango.sowing_season: Planting: February – March or July – August (grafted plants preferred; seedlings are not recommended for commercial orchards)
mango.harvesting_season: May – August (varies by variety — early: Sindhri in May; mid: Chaunsa in June–July; late: Anwar Ratol, S.B. Chaunsa in July–August)
mango.water_needs: Moderate once established; young trees need regular watering every 7–10 days. Mature trees benefit from irrigation during flowering and fruit development (February – May). Reduce watering after monsoon to encourage dormancy and next year's flowering.
common_issues: Mango Sudden Death Syndrome (MSDS / Ceratocystis) — rapid wilting and death of trees; a serious threat in Pakistani orchards
Anthracnose — black spots on leaves, flowers, and fruits; worsens in humid weather
Powdery Mildew (Ampheli) — white powdery growth on flowers and young fruits, causes fruit drop
Mango Fruit Fly (Bactrocera) — larvae tunnel into ripening fruits, making them unfit for market
Hoppers / Mealybugs — sap-sucking insects on flower panicles that reduce fruit set
mango.fertilizer_tip: General NPK guidance for a bearing tree (age 10+ years): apply ~2 kg N + 1 kg P₂O₅ + 2 kg K₂O per tree per year, split into two doses: one before flowering (January) and one after fruit set (April). Add 50–100 kg well-decomposed FYM per tree annually. Adjust doses based on tree age and soil test.
general_tips: Plant grafted plants of recommended varieties (Sindhri, Chaunsa, Anwar Ratol, S.B. Chaunsa, Fajri) from a reputable nursery — grafted trees bear fruit in 3–4 years vs. 7–10 years for seedlings.
Prune trees annually after harvest to maintain an open canopy — this improves light penetration, reduces disease, and makes spraying and picking easier.
Use fruit fly traps (methyl eugenol) from flowering onwards to monitor and reduce fruit fly populations; bag individual fruits for export-quality production.
